concepts.decision: Start with a protected asset and measurable need, not a preferred product.
concepts.definition: Testable statements of the protection property, asset, constraints, and owner.
concepts.failureExample: “Make it secure” gives no property, threat, or acceptance condition.
concepts.label: Security Requirements

concepts.decision: Compare options by coverage, dependencies, operation, evidence, and residual risk.
concepts.definition: Choosing safeguards that address a stated threat path within constraints.
concepts.failureExample: A team buys an endpoint tool for an API authorization failure.
concepts.label: Control Selection

concepts.decision: Use as a starting floor; tailor with documented risk and compensating measures.
concepts.definition: Minimum set of safeguards expected for a system class or risk level.
concepts.failureExample: A high-impact system adopts a generic workstation baseline unchanged.
concepts.label: Control Baseline

concepts.decision: Use where blocking is feasible and the false-denial cost is acceptable.
concepts.definition: Control intended to stop an unwanted event before it succeeds.
concepts.failureExample: MFA blocks use of a stolen password before a session begins.
concepts.label: Preventive Control

concepts.decision: Use when prevention cannot be complete and timely visibility changes outcome.
concepts.definition: Control that reveals an event or condition for investigation or response.
concepts.failureExample: Protected audit logs reveal abnormal privileged access after it occurs.
concepts.label: Detective Control

concepts.decision: Use where repair, reconfiguration, or cleanup reduces consequence.
concepts.definition: Control that restores an acceptable condition after an event or defect.
concepts.failureExample: A tested rebuild removes malware from a compromised endpoint.
concepts.label: Corrective Control

concepts.decision: Approve only with reason, scope, evidence, owner, and review date.
concepts.definition: Alternative safeguard that achieves comparable risk reduction when the preferred control cannot be used.
concepts.failureExample: A legacy device cannot run an agent, so isolation and monitored jump access are used.
concepts.label: Compensating Control

concepts.decision: Require tests, monitoring, and records tied to the control objective.
concepts.definition: Evidence-based confidence that a control is designed and operating as intended.
concepts.failureExample: A control exists in a diagram but fails after configuration drift.
concepts.label: Assurance

concepts.decision: Escalate when remaining exposure exceeds the authorized risk tolerance.
concepts.definition: Risk remaining after selected controls and accepted constraints.
concepts.failureExample: A service remains internet-exposed after mitigations but no owner accepts the risk.
concepts.label: Residual Risk

misconceptions.claim: A control is selected once and then remains suitable forever.
misconceptions.correction: Changes in threat, architecture, operation, and requirements require reassessment.

outcome: Trace a security requirement to a proportionate control set, evidence, owner, and residual-risk decision.

sections.body: Translate a business need into confidentiality, integrity, availability, privacy, safety, or accountability requirements; identify threats, architecture constraints, and risk tolerance; then select preventive, detective, corrective, recovery, or compensating controls. Consider control dependencies and avoid a single point of failure. A requirement should also state an owner, measurable expectation, and acceptable exception process.
keyPoints: Controls are treatments for defined risk and requirements.
A compensating control must address the relevant failure, not merely exist nearby.
sections.title: Derive controls from a requirement

sections.body: Document why a control was selected, how it is configured, what assumptions it relies on, and what evidence demonstrates effective operation. Test behavior under expected failures and changes, monitor drift, and reassess residual risk. This connects Domain 1 governance and risk decisions with Domain 6 assessment and Domain 7 operational evidence.
keyPoints: A designed control and an operating control are separate claims.
Requirements change as assets, threats, laws, and business processes change.
sections.title: Validate design and operation

sections.body: Translate a system requirement into a protected asset or service, property, threat or failure, constraint, owner, control objective, implementation option, evidence, and residual risk. Combine administrative, technical, and physical controls as needed; choose preventive, detective, corrective, deterrent, compensating, or recovery roles based on the path rather than product category. Consider feasibility, interoperability, performance, human operation, lifecycle cost, privacy, supplier dependency, and failure behavior. Assess control design and operation through tests and monitoring, and document exceptions with accountable risk acceptance. Failure modes include copying a framework baseline without tailoring, selecting a control that an operator cannot sustain, or measuring deployment instead of the intended reduction in risk.
keyPoints: State the protected property, boundary, decision owner, operating evidence, and residual failure mode.
Treat architecture controls as lifecycle commitments: configuration, monitoring, response, maintenance, and recovery determine whether the claim holds.

learningJob.plainExplanation: Controls should follow the stated requirement and interrupt its credible failure path. Operating and test evidence support the residual-risk decision; control strength is irrelevant when the mechanism addresses another property.
